items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I believe one of your most recent recordings was a Gershwin collection?

ctx.x: Well, I learned early on that the more things I could do, the more I’d be called to work, and making a living is a very big factor for all of us. So I was pleased to learn organ and be on call for all kinds of peculiar, non-jazz organ things, and played piano in very odd situations indeed, and arranging began to come around because I was so active every other way so I began to be the arranger and conductor on dates. But you’ve asked whether, what I really liked to do. And I think that early on and finally in a…

I believe one of your most recent recordings was a Gershwin collection? I’m curious as to, from a technical standpoint, what have you found was one of your most challenging prospects? Because when you record Scott Joplin, this is music that’s pretty much written out, yet it has to be played like it doesn’t sound like it’s written.

I think that all piano music, not just jazz, not just Scott Joplin, but classical music in general, it should sound as though the performer is improvising it. That’s what I think. And at its best, in my judgment, I can convince myself in an irrational way, that that is happening. And if you hear Mozart played that way, it sounds like the performer might be improvising it. We know they’re not. But there are aspects of performance that even people who are playing note for note understand. And it has to sound as…
